title: In the (Book) Club: Vol 3
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: In the third installment of an ongoing book-club series, the author reviews four education and psychology books alongside two Australian research papers, arguing that reading widely lets one book's core idea connect to and reinforce another's rather than treating any single text as the definitive answer to teaching. The book selections span Carl Hendrick and Robin MacPherson's expert-interview format on classroom-applicable neuroscience, David Didau and Nick Rose's three-part treatment of learning psychology and its professional controversies, Kahneman's System 1/System 2 framework with its glycogen-depletion experiment, and Haili Hughes's practical mentoring framework built around explicit, section-by-section teacher standards. The two research papers reviewed carry concrete, quotable findings: Blaise Joseph's survey work quantifying disruptive behaviour as roughly nine minutes lost per thirty-minute lesson, amounting to twelve weeks of instructional time per year, and AERO's literature review finding writing instruction confidence declines precisely as teachers move into the senior cohorts who most need strong writing instruction. The entry closes by tying both papers back to Carl Hendrick's gardening-versus-biology metaphor for the current state of writing pedagogy - practiced more than it is understood.
points: Treats book selection itself as a curriculum-design exercise, deliberately choosing titles whose frameworks (System 1/2, cognitive load, mentoring standards) interlock into a single reinforcing schema rather than standing alone.

Extracts a specific, quantified cost of classroom disruption from Blaise Joseph's survey research - roughly nine minutes lost per thirty-minute lesson, compounding to twelve weeks of lost instructional time per year - turning a familiar complaint into a measurable stake.

Surfaces a structural irony from AERO's writing-instruction literature review: teacher confidence in teaching writing declines specifically as students move into senior cohorts, meaning the students who most need sophisticated writing instruction are taught by the least confident teachers.

Uses Kahneman's glycogen-depletion experiment (sweetened vs. artificially sweetened drinks affecting sustained System 2 focus) as a concrete, memorable illustration of cognitive load rather than an abstract claim.

Frames Haili Hughes's mentoring framework by its section-by-section, directly implementable structure (high expectations, subject knowledge, behaviour management, assessment) rather than as a general endorsement, making it usable for whoever is currently mentoring a specific pre-service or graduate teacher.
